name: David Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior wok cook at Jade Garden, a Cantonese place on Harbour Road that does maybe four hundred covers on a Saturday. I'm in at ten to check the deliveries, then I break down the pork shoulders and get the stocks going before the lunch rush. From twelve it's three woks going at once, tickets screaming, and I'm calling the pass for the two junior cooks next to me. What I love is the wok itself, that smoky taste you only get from a real flame. What wears me out is the heat and the double shifts when someone calls in sick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you call the pass for the junior cooks. What does that part of the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means I'm the one deciding what goes out and when, so table nine's noodles don't sit dying while the duck is still cutting. I train the new ones too, like Kwame, who started in March and still burns the garlic when it gets busy. I don't use any apps or tablets for that, it's all shouting and paper tickets on the rail. Lena, my partner, says I come home hoarse three nights a week. She's a nurse, so between her nights and my evenings we mostly see each other on Mondays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the bosses were promised a miracle and got a fancy calculator. At the union meeting I'd probably make a joke about it. Nobody in my kitchen uses AI anyway, so there wouldn't be much to talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would be a relief, but it doesn't fix my real problems. Our rent on the flat went up eight percent this year, and Jade Garden's owner keeps talking about rising costs. So I'd still be watching every rota to see if my hours get trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep running the wok station, keep pushing the owner to sign the union's sick pay deal, and keep the savings we have, about four months, where they are. Maybe Lena and I would finally book the trip to her sister's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, a bit tired. The worry isn't robots, it's whether the restaurant has a slow winter and cuts staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the owner talking about rising costs. What would that mean for you if things stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Lau (his boss) already cut one kitchen porter last year, so the dishes land on us at the end of the night. If he trims more, it's me doing two jobs for one wage. Robots aren't what scares a cook like me. A slow January and a boss counting every hour on the rota scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And how sure are you that your own job is safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty sure. Good wok cooks are hard to find, and I'm the one who trains everyone. If Jade Garden went under, there are other places on Harbour Road that would take me, maybe not at the same pay.

say: AI is a **fancy calculator** that the bosses overpaid for, and nothing changed in our kitchen.
The real fight is still **sick pay** and fair hours, not robots.
think: My **job is safe** because good wok cooks are rare and I train everyone.
The pressure is **rent** and a slow winter that could trim my **hours**.
do: **Keep running** the wok station and training the junior cooks as usual.
**Push** the owner, with the union, to sign the sick pay deal.
**Leave** the four months of savings untouched and maybe book a family trip.
feel: Mostly **normal**, with a low hum of worry about a **slow winter**.
S0.quote: Robots aren't what scares a cook like me. A slow January and a boss counting every hour on the rota scare me.
fieldNote: He brushed off AI fast; his real worry is **rent** up eight percent and a boss trimming the rota.
Talks about the **union** as the natural place to take problems, even small ones.
Confident in his **skill**, but knows other jobs nearby might pay less.

steps.text: Keep running the wok station and training Kwame through the busy shifts
Press Mr Lau with the union to sign the sick pay deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union branch that this is exactly when we need rules, before the owners buy anything. Online I'd share the stuff about delivery apps squeezing restaurants, because that's already happening. I'd say a cook's hands aren't going anywhere for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine for now, because nobody is building a robot that tosses a wok properly. But the ordering and the rota would go to software, and that's the part that decides my hours. If a program says Tuesday lunch needs one cook, then it's one cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that no rota software cuts hours without talking to staff first. I'd keep cooking the same way, no tablets for me. And I'd start putting a bit more aside, maybe an extra hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but I'd be watching people around me get squeezed, like the front-of-house girls who take bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no tablets for you. What if the owner asked you to use the new ordering system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, but I'd hate it, and I'd let the junior cooks handle the screen. I learned this trade with my hands and my nose. I don't want a tablet telling me when the stock is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei-Ling, who runs the bookings and the phones out front. If AI answers customers and books tables, that's her whole job. She's been there eleven years, and she's the reason half the regulars come back.

say: This is when we need **union rules**, before the owners buy anything.
A cook's **hands** aren't going anywhere for a while.
think: My **cooking** is safe, but the **rota software** would decide my hours.
Staff who take **bookings** out front would feel this long before the kitchen does.
do: **Attend** every union meeting and push for consultation before any rota software cuts hours.
**Save** an extra hundred a month on top of the current cushion.
**Keep** cooking the old way and leave any new screens to the juniors.
feel: **Uneasy**, because my job looks fine while the people around me get **squeezed**.
S1.quote: I learned this trade with my hands and my nose. I don't want a tablet telling me when the stock is ready.
fieldNote: Sees the threat to cooks coming through **software** that sets hours, not through robots at the stove.
Strong **dislike** of tablets; would use one only if forced.
Worries more about **Mei-Ling** at the front desk than about himself.

steps.text: Push at union meetings for staff consultation before any rota software
Put an extra hundred a month into the joint savings
Keep cooking by hand and leave the ordering tablet to juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the bosses' dream, a kitchen with no wages, and we need laws now before 2031. I'd be posting union petitions every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. The thinking stuff, the ordering and rotas and booking, goes in 2028, and I don't care much about that. But three years later a robot that cooks as well as me? I'd be thirty-one with nothing but a cooking certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent or food and push our savings from four months to eight. I'd go to the union and push for a deal that any robot in the kitchen comes with retraining paid by the owner. I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a little. Like watching a wave and having nowhere to run, because I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd still be cooking in 2029 and 2030, maybe even busier, because the owners would cut the office stuff first. But I'd know the clock is ticking. Three years of cooking with a countdown over the stove is no gift. It just means I watch the end coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never touch a tablet. Would that change if the robots were coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd learn enough to fix the machines, I don't know. Lena keeps saying I should look at it, but I've never been good with screens. I'd probably dig in at the union instead, that's where I'm useful.

say: This is the bosses' dream of a **kitchen with no wages**, and we need laws before 2031.
Every cook should sign the **union petitions** now.
think: The thinking work goes in 2028, but **robots by 2031** reach my actual job.
At thirty-one I'd have **only a cooking certificate** and no other trade.
do: **Cut** spending to rent and food and grow savings to **eight months**.
**Push** the union for owner-paid retraining whenever a robot comes into a kitchen.
**Vote** for parties promising a **basic income** and stronger worker protection.
feel: **Sick** and trapped, like watching a wave with **nowhere to run**.
S2.quote: Three years of cooking with a countdown over the stove is no gift. It just means I watch the end coming.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** feels like a countdown to him, not breathing room.
Won't retrain toward tech; turns to the **union** and politics instead.
Gap between public anger and private **fear** of having no other skill.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and pause the family trip
Grow the joint savings from four to eight months of costs
Push the union for owner-paid retraining whenever robots arrive
Vote for parties promising a basic income for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's use them. At the union I'd be the one asking for a robot tax to pay for cooks who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but it lands in the same place. By 2034 I'd be thirty-four, and that's still young enough to be thrown out with no pension worth anything. The office side of the restaurant changes in 2031, and by then I'd already see owners pricing up robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking, keep saving, maybe two hundred a month extra. I'd take on a role at the union branch, maybe shop steward for the restaurants on Harbour Road. Lena says I should do a course, and maybe I'd look at food safety inspection, something with a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. There's time to fight, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why food safety inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to sign off that the food is safe, and I'd guess the law keeps a person on that longer than on the wok. It uses what I know. I'd rather check a robot kitchen for rats than stand next to a robot pretending I'm still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a union role. What would you actually push for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot tax, first, so owners who replace cooks pay into a fund. And a rule that long-serving staff get first pick of any new jobs, like running or cleaning the machines. Kwame and the young ones would need it more than me.

say: We've got **five years** to get the rules right, so let's use them.
Owners who replace cooks should pay a **robot tax**.
think: Five years only delays it; by **2034** I'd be thrown out at thirty-four.
Owners would be **pricing robots** as soon as the office work goes in 2031.
do: **Save** about two hundred a month extra while the job still pays.
**Stand** as shop steward for the restaurants on Harbour Road.
**Look** into a food safety inspection course, a licensed job.
S3.quote: I'd rather check a robot kitchen for rats than stand next to a robot pretending I'm still needed.
fieldNote: More time makes him consider **retraining**, but only toward a licensed, rule-protected job.
Union work is his **identity**; he wants a formal role.
Thinks about **younger cooks** as the ones most at risk.

steps.text: Save two hundred extra a month into the joint account
Stand for shop steward for the Harbour Road restaurants
Ask about a food safety inspector course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to plan properly, so there's no excuse for governments to leave cooks behind. I'd keep the union pushing the same things, just with less panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably relax for the first few years, which is maybe the wrong thing. Robots in 2039, I'm thirty-nine then, and that's still a long way off in kitchen years. But I know myself, I'd put off changing until it was too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Jade Garden or somewhere like it, and keep saving steadily. I'd stay active in the union. Anything bigger, like retraining, I'd wait and see how the first robots actually work in kitchens before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried underneath, and a bit guilty, because I know I'd use the time badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the time badly. What would using it well look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Using it well would be doing a course now, while I'm young and have no kids. Lena would tell me that over dinner every Monday. Ten years sounds like forever to a cook. Ask any chef, we can't plan past Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot actually cook well in a real restaurant nearby. Until then, it's just stories on the news. If I saw one on Harbour Road, I'd move.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time, so governments have **no excuse** to leave cooks behind.
The union should keep pushing, just with **less panic**.
think: Robots in **2039** feel far off, so I'd probably **put off** changing.
The end point is the same; I'd still be **thirty-nine** with one trade.
do: **Keep cooking** and saving steadily at Jade Garden or a similar kitchen.
**Wait** to see real kitchen robots before deciding on retraining.
feel: A steady **worry**, and a bit **guilty** that I'd waste the time.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever to a cook. Ask any chef, we can't plan past Saturday night.
fieldNote: Admits he would **procrastinate** with a decade of warning.
His trigger to act is **seeing a robot** cook well nearby, not news stories.
Still expects to **lose the job** eventually, which keeps a steady worry under the calm talk.

steps.text: Keep cooking at Jade Garden and saving a little each month
Stay on the union branch committee for the restaurants
Wait until a robot cooks on Harbour Road before retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years for the office stuff and five for the robots is no time for someone like me, who only knows the wok. What would help is the union actually having teeth, and a law that owners who bring in robots pay for the cooks they replace. Cooks don't need pity. We need a law that says the owner who buys the robot pays for the cook it replaces.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones. Kwame is nineteen and thinks he has a career ahead of him. I'd want someone to be honest with kids like him before they spend years learning a trade that might not last.

headlineQuote: Cooks don't need pity. We need a law that says the owner who buys the robot pays for the cook it replaces.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** senior wok cook at a busy Cantonese restaurant, living with his partner, a nurse.
He's **union-minded**, never uses AI tools, and loves the craft of cooking over a real flame.
In AI Plateau his worries are **rent** and trimmed hours; in Steady Disruption, rota software.
The fast **AGI** picture alarms him, because robots arrive while he has only one trade.
With more warning he admits he'd **put off** change and lean on the union instead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years for office work and five for robots leaves him no time.
whatWouldHelp: A union with **real power** and a law that makes owners **pay** for the cooks they replace.
